S1.title: 429 Too Many Requests - HTTP | MDN
S1.excerpt:
The HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` client error response status code indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. This mechanism of asking the client to slow down the rate of requests is commonly called "rate limiting".

A `Retry-After` header may be included to this response to indicate how long a client should wait before making the request again. [...] http

```
GET /reports/mdn HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com 
```

In this example, server-wide rate limiting is active when a client exceeds a set threshold of requests per minute. A 429 response is returned with a `Retry-After` header that indicates requests will be allowed for this client again after 3600 seconds (60 minutes):

http

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests Content-Type: text/html Retry-After: 3600   Too Many Requests

# Too Many Requests

You're doing that too often! Try again later. [...] Implementations of rate limiting vary; restrictions may be server-wide or per resource. Typically, rate-limiting restrictions are based on a client's IP but can be specific to users or authorized applications if requests are authenticated or contain a cookie.
```

```
S2.title: Retry-After header - HTTP | MDN
S2.excerpt:
In a `503 Service Unavailable` response, this indicates how long the service is expected to be unavailable.
 In a `429 Too Many Requests` response, this indicates how long to wait before making a new request.
 In a redirect response, such as `301 Moved Permanently`, this indicates the minimum time that the user agent is asked to wait before issuing the redirected request.
```

```
## Directives [...] Support for the `Retry-After` header on both clients and servers is still inconsistent. However, some crawlers and spiders, like the Googlebot, honor the `Retry-After` header. It is useful to send it along with a `503` response, so that search engines will keep indexing your site when the downtime is over.

http

```
Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT Retry-After: 120 

Have you ever wondered how APIs politely tell clients to “slow down” or “come back later”? That’s where the Retry-After HTTP header comes into play. Whether you're building a rate-limited API, implementing graceful degradation during server maintenance, or creating resilient client applications, understanding the Retry-After header is crucial.

bundles.question: For the HTTP status code 429 (Too Many Requests), which RFC defines it, what the status means, and which response header tells the client how long to wait before retrying?
bundles.summary:
- **RFC defining HTTP 429**: **RFC 6585** (“Additional HTTP Status Codes”) defines **429 Too Many Requests** [https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6585].
- **Meaning of status 429**: **429 Too Many Requests** indicates the client has sent **too many requests in a given amount of time**, and the server is effectively **rate limiting** by asking the client to slow down [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429].
- **Response header for retry timing**: The **`Retry-After`** response header indicates **how long the client should wait before making a follow-up request** after receiving 429 [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/429] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Retry-After].
